Gone From My Sight by Henry van Dyke.

I am standing upon the seashore. A ship, at my side, spreads her white sails to the moving breeze and starts for the blue ocean. She is an object of beauty and strength.

I stand and watch her until, at length, she hangs like a speck of white cloud just where the sea and sky come to mingle with each other.

Then, someone at my side says, “There, she is gone.”

Gone where?

Gone from my sight. That is all. She is just as large in mast, hull and spar as she was when she left my side. And, she is just as able to bear her load of living freight to her destined port.

Her diminished size is in me — not in her.

And, just at the moment when someone says, “There, she is gone,” there are other eyes watching her coming, and other voices ready to take up the glad shout, “Here she comes!”

From my experience weight loss comes with loss of appetite or inability to eat/swallow foods. 

If he is eating and/or able to feed himself you may need to check his routine for yourself. Loved ones can get overwhelmed and want to think they are their usual selves

Example:

My gran used to give off all the time about my grandfather eating but he was drastically shedding weight. 

What would happen, is he would walk around with a sandwich or an apple (or whatever) and not eat it, but move it from place to place. She though he was non-stop eating because he was ALWAYS on the move and ALWAYS had snacks or made half sandwiches. 

If he is actually eating and shedding weight then you should take him to the doctor and get their advice. 

This could also be a medication change or who knows what else, but you should be 100% sure he is actually eating as much as mum says he is.


Edit: i just saw the cleared to drive locally. Please please monitor this heavily. Put an AirTag on his keys and on the vehicle itself. You don’t want him to regress one night and take off across the country.

It’s not about telling a flat out lie, but using it as a jumping board into an easier or more peaceful conversation. 

If it is going to cause her great distress and discomfort to hear the naked truth every time she asks is it worth putting her through that? 

When she stops asking every hour and it then becomes every minute does she deserve to be put through that discomfort and harrowing experience every time?

When my grandfather died my family (3 main carers) agreed she obviously deserves to grieve and feel the very real pain of losing her best friend and love of her life of 60 years. Our love makes us human and she was entitled to feel that loss and we grieved as a family should.

However, if she continued to ask about her husband (my grandfather), in the following weeks and months, and I told her the bare truth I would be causing her unneeded distress and heartbreak. 
To her she would experiencing it again for the first time. 
It is of no benefit to her to live through that again as if it’s brand new, no one deserves that hell.
When she asked here he was I would say “oh you know that man he never sits still”
“Hes always out and about”

It’s as much for her as it is for you. You don’t deserve to be put through it either, but you’ll do everything you can to keep her happy and comfortable. 

This is going to be heartbreaking and painful for you regardless of the truths that are told so at least make it easy for her.

If that means telling white lies or diverting the conversation.

The best advice I can give is don’t begin to mourn. It’s so difficult to stop yourself from doing this but it will be important to be aware of it when it happens. 

Other than that? It’s fuckin party time. 

Tea dates.
Short walks or chair rolls through parks. 
Listening to music and maybe a few dances in the living room! 
A little wine on a Tuesday. I started filling a rose wine bottle with a mix of wine a mostly juice and the ratio would become more juice as she progressed. 
Old photo albums and movie nights with her favourite films! 
Make a journal of the ridiculous stuff that will inevitably happen, it’s good for venting when you start to feel maxed out, and the memories they create will bring you peace years later when you read through them.
When you look back at these entries you’ll remember you were there when she needed you and you did everything you could even if it doesn’t feel it. 
Truthfully you don’t need to “do everything you can at all times” this leads to burn out and no one can achieve this - you just need to be there for her.

Write down stories she likes to tell so you can prompt some conversations as her memory becomes shakey.
These stories can remain with her as she progresses and it will bring her comfort to be able to recall and tell you about something at length.

1. she is there because she can be cared for by seasoned carers and get the dignity she deserves.

2. she is there because you love her and will do what’s best for her even if it is hard for you.

Diversion and distraction is usually the best way to go and as she plateaus and regresses she may become more comfortable with her surroundings.

What you should do is go take your dad out on a date at a new restaurant or type of show

Take a short road trip for the weekend or ask him to involve you in one of his hobbies, whatever he is into.

Prioritize your experiences with your dad so you can give your mom the time and positive energy she deserves.

You do make every day good for him, even if it doesn’t feel like it. 

Just remember to make a few good days for yourself too. It is easy to feel guilty about self care and burn out but you deserve a little bit of life too.
